title: 23 Bell Ringers Teachers Love
author: Andrea Tamayo
summary: Andrea Tamayo compiles 23 teacher-tested bell ringers for Edutopia, drawn from nearly 400 educator responses to a social media callout. The framing argument is that the best openers are not busywork to fill attendance time but intentional tasks that reactivate prior knowledge, preview the day's learning and prime discussion, a point she anchors with a teacher's reminder that a bell ringer should support the lesson. The collection spans subjects and grade levels and varies in length and format. Many entries are retrieval and reasoning tasks: Which One Doesn't Belong vocabulary sets, My Favorite No error analysis, deliberate Find the Mistake problems, collaborative brain dumps, quick card sorts and Mystery Number clues. Others emphasize discussion and relationship-building (Inside-Outside Circle, Board Splash, Rankings of character responsibility), observation (Think-Notice-Wonder, artifacts, detailed art images) and settling routines (mindful journaling, silent reading, morning jobs). Each is attributed to a named practitioner with a concrete example, making the piece a practical menu rather than an argument.
points: The piece's organizing principle is that bell ringers should be intentional retrieval or preview tasks tied to the lesson, not time-fillers during attendance.
Error-focused openers (My Favorite No, Find the Mistake) turn common misconceptions into discussion, and the article shows this works beyond math, for example in civics.
Tasks without a single correct answer, such as Which One Doesn't Belong or ranking characters' responsibility in Romeo and Juliet, force students to justify reasoning.
Collaborative brain dumps are highlighted as a way to ensure every student participates in retrieving the previous day's learning.
Some entries prioritize regulation and belonging (mindful journaling, silent reading, classroom jobs), showing bell ringers can also manage transitions.
quotes: The strongest bell ringers, teachers say, do more than just occupy students while they take attendance. Used thoughtfully, bell ringers can reactivate prior knowledge, preview the day’s learning, and lay the groundwork for lively discussions.

Earth science teacher Emily May gives students four vocabulary terms—such as “evaporation,” “condensation,” “sublimation,” and “freezing”—and asks them to decide which one doesn’t belong and explain why. Because there isn’t always one correct answer, students must think carefully about how the concepts relate.
Collect their work and sort into piles of right answers (“Yes”) and wrong answers (“No”). Pick out a “No” that demonstrates a common error and discuss with the class how to go about correcting it.

Get students retrieving the previous day’s learning by asking small groups to write down everything they remember on a whiteboard or sheet of paper. One student begins, then passes it to a classmate to add anything they missed.
Searching for the error gets students discussing relevant material right at the start of class and reasoning through why the answer is wrong, she writes on Facebook.
The activity helps students recognize shades of meaning rather than treating all synonyms as interchangeable, explains teacher Michelle Krause on Facebook.
Project an artifact from the period that students are studying—such as a photograph, piece of clothing, or tool—and ask what historians could learn from it, as well as what it might leave unanswered.
